source.book: The Art and Science of Technical Analysis
source.author: Adam Grimes

conventions: stop and limit entries mechanized as bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; price-level conditions rejected (shift test)

rejected.quote: there is a bid price at which buyers are willing to buy an asset, an offer (or ask...) at which sellers are offering to sell, and usually a last print (or simply, last) price where a trade was made... the distance between those two prices is often referred to as the spread.
rejected.reason: requires live bid/ask quote data below the bar; the engine has only OHLCV

rejected.quote: If stock XYZ last printed 50.00 three weeks ago, but is now bid at 30.00 and offered at 49.00, what is it actually worth?... a major factor in the 2007-2008 financial crisis was the importance of many financial instruments representing very significant financial commitments that did not have liquid markets.
rejected.reason: market-microstructure/liquidity narrative with no bar-level test; illiquid quote behavior isn't representable from OHLCV bars

rejected.quote: By analyzing the number of orders that hit the bid (seller-motivated trades) compared to those that take the offer (buyer-motivated trades)... traders can get a deeper sense of the conviction levels and urgency behind price moves.
rejected.reason: requires tick-level trade-side (buyer- vs seller-motivated) classification data below the bar

rejected.quote: Spread trading is another type of transaction involving buying one asset and selling another, looking to profit from the change in value between the two.
rejected.reason: requires a second instrument/spread leg; the engine trades one symbol

rejected.quote: The most primitive type of chart would simply be the information in the prints plotted on a graph with price on the y-axis and trade number on the x-axis... a single-tick chart of the market's opening for Apple, Inc.
rejected.reason: tick/trade-count chart construction below the bar; not a bar-level condition and not data the engine has

rejected.quote: it is possible to aggregate bars not by ticks (transactions) but by trading volume... Another possibility is to have each bar end after a certain range is reached... range bars created at the end of a trading day will be different from the ones created as the market unfolds. This makes backtesting and analysis on range bars virtually impossible.
rejected.reason: alternate bar-construction schemes (volume bars, range bars) below the engine's fixed-timeframe OHLCV bars; Grimes himself states range bars are unusable for backtesting

rejected.quote: Market Profile charts essentially allow the trader to look inside the bar to see where most volume and trading activity occurred in the time period... with wider horizontal bars indicating more trading activity at that price level.
rejected.reason: requires intrabar volume-at-price (TPO) data the engine does not have

rejected.quote: Traders often find it useful to mark the first trade of the period with a tick on the left side of the bar (the open) and the last trade of the period with a tick on the right side (the close). These four data points, plotted like this, create the classical bar chart.
rejected.reason: defines the OHLC bar itself, which the engine already receives as input; not a trading condition

chapter_summary: Appendix A is a market-microstructure and order-mechanics primer: bid/ask spread, market makers, limit vs market orders, long/short and spread trading, and a survey of chart types (tick, time, volume, range-bar, candlestick, Market Profile). None of it states a bar-level entry/exit/context condition the engine could evaluate; everything either needs data the engine does not have (bid/ask, tick-level trade side, another instrument, intrabar volume-at-price) or simply defines terms (the OHLC bar itself, long vs short) rather than a rule. Recorded zero candidates; the rejected list below covers the chapter's content so the dedup pass knows nothing was skipped by omission.
